Glossary

Related terms: UF = also called; BT = broader term; NT = narrower term; RT = related term.

TermWhat it meansRelated termsExample, from this register
CapabilityWhat the business is able to do, named apart from how it is built. Covered by the flows that deliver it.Fulfil customer orders
Intended flowOne case's path from start to end, as designed.Fulfilling a customer's order
StageOne ordered stretch of a flow, with an entry and an exit.RT State · RT StatusPlace the order
Process stepOne act inside a stage, with an outcome the business would recognise, that happened or did not.RT Operation (of a part)The customer's basket is emptied
PartA person or a component that carries out or supports a process step: anything that carries a process step, an AI agent included.UF participant · NT ComponentFulfilment staff; WebApp
ComponentA deployable the flow's process steps run through whose code can be had, whatever its application, repository or team. An AI agent is one.BT Part · RT External dependency · RT Operation (of a part)WebApp
External dependencyA deployable the flow relies on whose code cannot be had: a vendor, a hosted service, a repository with no access. Seen from the calling side; it can still perform a process step.RT ComponentWebhook subscriber endpoint
Operation (of a part)A tool, route or handler a component offers, joined to the process steps it serves. Not a code module.RT Component · RT Process stepa route such as POST /api/orders, or a handler such as OrderStartedIntegrationEvent
Expected outcomeA way a stage ends on its main path: the case leaves the stage as designed. Not numbered.The order is placed
Other outcomeAny other way a stage ends: an alternative or exception path out of it. Not numbered.The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock
RunOne request an AI agent takes for one case, from taking it to its reply.UF agent invocation · RT Operation (in a run) · RT Agent part
Operation (in a run)One act inside a run: a call to its model, a tool, or a check. Not a process step.RT Run
Agent partA piece of the agent's own machinery: its model, the functions it may call, its guardrails or its orchestration.RT Run
CaseOne instance going through a flow, from its start to its end: what the business measures count.RT StateOne order
StateWhere one case stands in its lifecycle: one of the states it can be in and move between. A system records it as a status, or it is implicit where the case plainly waits and nothing records it.RT Status · RT Case · RT StageSubmitted
StatusThe value a system records and shows for a case's state. A data concern, not a stage: the two often line up but do not coincide, since a stage can span two statuses and a stage's process steps can leave the status unchanged.RT State · RT StageSubmitted
On recordA measure the register holds: proposed, or emitted by the code today. Never a reading.
Not assessedLooked for in the sources examined and not found, or not looked at. Never a finding that it is absent.

4 flows · 4 stages · 7 process steps · 6 outcomes · 16 parts · 1 external dependency

How this process step is carried out

Trigger
  • WebApp deletes the basket through Basket API by gRPC after the order call.
  • ClientApp clears its basket the same way.
Interactions, in order
  1. WebApp → Basket API: deletes the basket through Basket API by gRPC after the order call; ClientApp clears its basket the same way
  2. Ordering API → Event bus: OrderStartedIntegrationEvent; written with the order
  3. Event bus → Basket API: OrderStartedIntegrationEvent; via RabbitMQ exchange eshop_event_bus to queue Basket, which deletes the basket
Other recorded calls (order not recorded)
  • Basket API → Basket store: basket read and delete
  • ClientApp → Basket API: mobile app clears its basket by gRPC
Expected outcome
the buyer's basket is gone once the order exists (proposed)
If it does not happen

The basket keeps the ordered items and the customer may order them twice.

Two paths empty it: the WebApp after its call and Basket API on OrderStartedIntegrationEvent.

Timeouts

No timeout of its own.

The WebApp's basket delete is a gRPC call whose client is made by the HTTP client factory, so it carries the standard resilience handler: each attempt 10 seconds, up to 3 retries, 30 seconds in all.

Basket API's delete on OrderStartedIntegrationEvent has no clock: the message waits in queue Basket until it is consumed, and the queue sets no expiry.

Trigger
WebApp reads the basket from Basket API by gRPC and the items' names and prices from Catalog API
Interactions, in order
  1. WebApp → Basket API: gRPC basket read at checkout and delete after the order call
  2. WebApp → Catalog API: catalogue items' names and prices for the basket lines
  3. WebApp → Ordering API: POST /api/orders; POST /api/orders with x-requestid, or ClientApp through Mobile BFF
  4. Ordering API → Ordering database: writes the order in Submitted with its buyer and payment method, and the OrderStarted and OrderStatusChangedToSubmitted outbox rows, in one transaction
Other recorded calls (order not recorded)
  • ClientApp → Mobile BFF: POST and PUT /api/orders/cancel from the mobile app
  • Mobile BFF → Ordering API: route /api/orders/{*any} to Ordering API
  • Basket API → Basket store: basket read and delete
  • Catalog API → Catalog database: item lookups per order line and outbox write
  • Ordering API → Identity API: token validation keys fetched by the JWT handler from its Authority
Expected outcome
an ordering.orders row in Submitted with one orderItems row per basket line at the catalogue price, the delivery address, and BuyerId and PaymentMethodId set (proposed)
If it does not happen

No order record.

  • Ordering API answers 200 even when the command returned false, and an exception inside the command is swallowed into false.
  • The WebApp does not read the response, empties the basket anyway and shows the orders page.

The customer must notice and order again.

Recovery
Not created
Timeouts
  • WebApp's HTTP clients carry the standard resilience handler.
  • A repeated POST with the same x-requestid is answered without a second order.

Trigger

Order Processor selects orders in Submitted older than the grace period, on every run.

The case is in Submitted.

Interactions, in order
  1. Order Processor → Ordering database: selects orders in Submitted older than the grace period, on every run
  2. Order Processor → Event bus: GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent
  3. Event bus → Ordering API: GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent; via RabbitMQ exchange eshop_event_bus to queue Ordering
  4. Ordering API → Ordering database: sets AwaitingValidation and writes OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent to its outbox in the same transaction
Expected outcome
Awaiting validation within 1.5 minutes of "OrderDate", with its OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidation outbox row at State 2 (Published) (proposed)
If it does not happen

The order stays in Submitted, and each poll publishes for it again, so it moves on once the poller, the broker and Ordering API's consumer work.

  • A failed query is logged and returns no orders.
  • A failed publish is not caught in the loop and stops the background service.
Recovery
Moves on
Timeouts

Grace period GracePeriodTime 1 minute, polled every CheckUpdateTime 30 seconds.

Every run re-publishes for each order still Submitted.

The bus's retry policy (RetryCount 10) never retries a failed publish: Execute is given an async lambda, so the failure lands in the returned task, not the call (Polly's Execute overloads).

Trigger

Ordering API publishes OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent from ordering."IntegrationEventLog" right after the commit.

The case is in Awaiting validation.

Interactions, in order
  1. Ordering API → Ordering database: order, buyer, status and outbox writes in one transaction
  2. Ordering API → Event bus: OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent; publishes from ordering."IntegrationEventLog" right after the commit
  3. Event bus → Catalog API: OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent; via RabbitMQ exchange eshop_event_bus to queue Catalog
  4. Catalog API → Catalog database: item lookups per order line and outbox write
  5. Catalog API: compares each item's AvailableStock with its units
  6. Catalog API → Catalog database: writes to its "IntegrationEventLog"
  7. Catalog API → Event bus: OrderStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent
  8. Event bus → Ordering API: OrderStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent; via RabbitMQ to queue Ordering
  9. Ordering API: waits 10 seconds
  10. Ordering API → Ordering database: sets StockConfirmed and writes OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent to its outbox
Expected outcome
  • Stock confirmed only when every ordered product is in the catalogue with AvailableStock of at least its units.
  • Description 'All the items were confirmed with available stock.' (proposed).
If it does not happen

The order stays in Awaiting validation with nothing to move it:

  • A failed publish is marked PublishedFailed and never sent again.
  • A consumer that throws still acknowledges the message, so it is gone.
  • The poll re-sends only for Submitted.

A message waiting in its queue for a stopped consumer moves on when the consumer returns.

Recovery
Stranded
Timeouts

10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set.

Ordering API consumes its queue with one consumer on one channel, so these waits queue behind one another.

Ordering API publishes OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent from ordering."IntegrationEventLog" right after the commit.

The case is in Stock confirmed.

Interactions, in order
  1. Ordering API → Ordering database: order, buyer, status and outbox writes in one transaction
  2. Ordering API → Event bus: OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent; publishes from ordering."IntegrationEventLog" right after the commit
  3. Event bus → Payment Processor: OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent; via RabbitMQ exchange eshop_event_bus to queue PaymentProcessor
  4. Payment Processor: decides from the setting PaymentOptions:PaymentSucceeded
  5. Payment Processor → Event bus: OrderPaymentSucceededIntegrationEvent
  6. Event bus → Ordering API: OrderPaymentSucceededIntegrationEvent; published directly with no outbox, via RabbitMQ to queue Ordering
  7. Ordering API: waits 10 seconds
  8. Ordering API → Ordering database: sets Paid and writes OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEvent to its outbox
Expected outcome
Paid, with the order total taken once from the buyer's payment method (proposed)
If it does not happen

The order stays in Stock confirmed with nothing to move it:

  • Ordering API's publish failure is marked PublishedFailed and never retried.
  • Payment Processor's publish has no outbox and its failure throws out of the handler, and every consumer acknowledges a message it failed on.

A message waiting in its queue for a stopped consumer moves on when the consumer returns.

Trigger

ClientApp to Mobile BFF: PUT /api/orders/cancel with x-requestid and the customer's token.

The case is in Submitted.

Interactions, in order
  1. ClientApp → Mobile BFF: PUT /api/orders/cancel with x-requestid and the customer's token
  2. Mobile BFF → Ordering API
  3. Ordering API → Ordering database: sets Cancelled and writes OrderStatusChangedToCancelledIntegrationEvent to its outbox
Other recorded calls (order not recorded)
  • Ordering API → Identity API: token validation keys fetched by the JWT handler from its Authority
Expected outcome
Cancelled before any payment is taken (proposed)
If it does not happen

The order is not cancelled and goes on along the main path.

  • Ordering API answers 500 'Cancel order failed to process.' when the command fails.
  • The mobile app treats only a 400 as a refusal.

The customer must try again.

Timeouts

No timeout of its own:

  • The mobile app's HttpClient has no handler, so it keeps .NET's default timeout of 100 seconds and makes one attempt.
  • Mobile BFF's route and Ordering API's cancel endpoint set none, and the cancel itself waits for nothing.

Trigger

OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEvent written with Paid, published after commit.

The case is in Paid.

Interactions, in order
  1. Ordering API → Event bus: OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEvent; written with Paid, published after commit
  2. Event bus → Catalog API: OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEvent; via RabbitMQ to queue Catalog
  3. Catalog API → Catalog database: removes each item's units from AvailableStock
Expected outcome
each item's AvailableStock reduced by its units (proposed)
If it does not happen

Stock is not reduced, and the next stock check confirms against the old figure.

RemoveStock throws for an item already at zero, the handler saves only after the loop, and the failed message is acknowledged and gone, so none of the order's items is reduced.

The order itself is unaffected.

Timeouts

No timeout:

  • The stock is reduced when Catalog API consumes the Paid event from queue Catalog.
  • No clock watches the message waiting there, and the queue sets no expiry.

Trigger

OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEvent.

The case is in Paid.

Interactions, in order
  1. Ordering API → Event bus: OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEvent
  2. Event bus → Webhooks API: OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEvent; via RabbitMQ to queue Webhooks
  3. Webhooks API → Webhook subscriber endpoint: POST of the event, once to each OrderPaid subscription's URL
Other recorded calls (order not recorded)
  • Webhooks API → Webhooks database: subscriptions read
Expected outcome
one post to each OrderPaid subscription, carrying the order's id and items (proposed)
If it does not happen

Subscribers are not told.

  • Each post is retried up to 3 times on a transient failure by the standard resilience handler every HTTP client carries, and its response is not read.
  • every OrderPaid subscription receives every order, with no filter by buyer.
Timeouts

Each post is bounded only by the standard resilience handler every HTTP client carries:

  • Each attempt 10 seconds, up to 3 retries, 30 seconds in all.
  • The posts to all subscriptions go out together and are awaited together.

No clock watches the message waiting in queue Webhooks.

someone ships the goods and records it.

The case is in Paid.

  1. Fulfilment staff: someone ships the goods and records it

If it does not happen

The order stays in Paid.

Nothing in the application calls the ship endpoint and no timer watches Paid orders: it is mapped and has no caller in WebApp, ClientApp or any worker.

Recovery
Stranded
Timeouts
No timeout: a person ships the goods and records it, and nothing in the application schedules or times that act

No record to count: The code records nothing after Shipped, so neither a delivery nor a failed or returned one is recorded
Cannot be undone
Does not apply: Its one recorded move tells webhook subscribers and does not change the order; shipping itself, which cannot be undone, is in stage ST3
At stake

  • For the whole flow:

    • Order id ("Id").
    • Order total (sum of Units x UnitPrice).
    • Items and units (ordering."orderItems").
    • Buyer (ordering.buyers "IdentityGuid").
    • Delivery address.
    • Payment method (card number masked to the last four digits).
Its alerts
  • Shipped orders not confirmed delivered within the expected time
Where this comes from
  • entry: Shipped: after the irreversible L13, waiting on the carrier (L14)
  • exit: implicit: delivered to the customer (not recorded by the code)
  • source: lifecycle L14; reference-model check: SCOR 12.0's Deliver process covers providing finished goods to meet demand, typically including transportation and distribution management (secondary source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supply_chain_operations_reference), work the code does not record; the code's last state is Shipped (Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/OrderStatus.cs:12)
  • The customer who placed the order: proposed: a shipped order reaches the customer; satisfied_when: proposed: the order delivered to the customer; the code records nothing after Shipped; source: measures.csv M301 alert; Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/OrderStatus.cs:12
  • L14: Shipped to Shipped, main; process step 4.1; Webhooks.API/IntegrationEvents/OrderStatusChangedToShippedIntegrationEventHandler.cs:8-17; Webhooks.API/Extensions/Extensions.cs:22

How a case moves end to end

Key to the drawing
  • Box: a stage, in order, with the time limit its code sets, where it sets one. Filled dot: where a case starts.
  • Arrow between stages: a case moves from one to the other. Solid: an expected outcome makes the move. Dashed: only an other outcome does.
  • Arc over a stage: a case can go straight past it, to the stage the arc ends at.
  • Dashed arrow down: an other outcome that ends the case in that stage.
  • Rounded box with a ringed dot: where the expected path ends.
One case
One order
Starts
The order's record is written in Submitted
Ends
The customer has the goods
Serves
  • The customer who placed the order: the customer has the goods, or is told definitively that the order will not be filled (proposed)
Delivers
  • Fulfil customer orders
  • Take and process customer orders
  • Notify outside parties of business events
Stage runbooks
  • Stage 1: Place the order
  • Stage 2: Accept the order
  • Stage 3: Ship the order
  • Stage 4: Deliver the order

  • ends_at: The customer has the goods: the order is delivered. The code's last recorded state is Shipped (Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/Order.cs:130-140; Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/OrderStatus.cs:12); the stretch to delivery is added from the reference model (ST4). Or definitively not: the order is Cancelled, for lack of stock (Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/Order.cs:155-168), a failed payment or the customer's request (Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/Order.cs:142-153)
